segments.text: Western feminist movements are conventionally divided into three (sometimes four) historical “waves,” a framework that is useful for organising the material but should be used carefully, since it can oversimplify continuous and overlapping activism into neat separate periods.
Why the wave framework exists.

Each “wave” is associated with a dominant set of demands, a dominant theoretical framework, and a period of heightened public visibility and mobilisation, even though feminist activity continued in the intervening periods at lower visibility.
Overview of the three main waves (each developed fully in Topics 19–21):

items.text: First wave
(roughly 1848–early 1900s): centred on legal and political rights, above all suffrage (the right to vote).
Second wave
(roughly 1960s–1980s): broadened the agenda to workplace equality, reproductive rights, sexuality, and the structural critique of patriarchy summarised in Topics 12–15.
Third wave
(roughly 1990s onward): emphasised diversity, intersectionality (Topic 17), and a critique of the earlier waves for centring the experiences of white, middle-class, heterosexual women.

segments.text: A fourth wave

is often now discussed, associated with digital-era activism (online movements such as #MeToo against sexual harassment and assault, beginning around 2017), though there is no full scholarly consensus on whether this constitutes a genuinely distinct wave or a continuation of the third wave using new tools.
Why examiners test this topic.

It requires linking each wave’s demands to the theoretical frameworks studied earlier (for example, first-wave suffrage campaigns drew on liberal feminist theory, Topic 12; second-wave critiques of the family and sexuality drew on radical feminism, Topic 13) — showing that theory and movement history are not separate topics but explain each other.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Western feminism is conventionally periodised into first, second, and third (and arguably fourth) waves, each with a dominant agenda.
The wave framework is a useful organising tool but risks oversimplifying continuous, overlapping activism.
Each wave’s demands connect directly to specific feminist theories covered in Topics 12–17.

segments.text: First-wave feminism spans roughly from the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention in the United States (widely treated as the symbolic beginning of organised feminist activism, where the Declaration of Sentiments demanded rights including suffrage) through the early twentieth century, when women won the right to vote in a series of countries — for example, New Zealand in 1893, Britain in stages between 1918 and 1928, and the United States in 1920 through the Nineteenth Amendment.
Core demands.

First-wave feminism concentrated on formal legal and political rights: the right to vote, the right to own property independently of a husband, the right to sign contracts, and access to higher education and certain professions previously closed to women. Its theoretical basis was primarily liberal feminism (Topic 12) — the argument that women, as rational individuals, deserved the same legal standing as men.
Key organisations and tactics.

Suffrage movements used petitioning, public marches, and — particularly in Britain through the more militant suffragette wing led by the Pankhursts — direct action including hunger strikes and property damage, alongside the more moderate “suffragist” wing that relied on lobbying and peaceful campaigning.
Limitations, important for critical evaluation.

First-wave feminism in most Western countries was led predominantly by white, middle- and upper-class women, and in several countries (including the United States) the right to vote in practice excluded women of colour for decades even after formal suffrage laws passed, due to other discriminatory barriers (such as racially targeted voting restrictions). This is a key point later feminists, especially third-wave and intersectional theorists (Topic 17), used to critique the movement’s limited scope.
Key Takeaways

items.text: First-wave feminism (c. 1848–early 1900s) focused on legal rights, above all suffrage, grounded in liberal feminist theory.
Seneca Falls (1848) is the conventional symbolic starting point; suffrage was achieved in stages across different countries between the 1890s and 1920s.
The movement is criticised for being led primarily by white, middle-class women, with rights not equally extended in practice to women of colour.

segments.text: Second-wave feminism runs roughly from the early 1960s to the 1980s and dramatically broadened feminism’s scope beyond formal legal rights to the structural and cultural roots of inequality.
Catalysts.

Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique (1963) is widely credited as a catalysing text, articulating the frustration of educated, middle-class American housewives confined to domestic roles despite formal legal equality — what Friedan called “the problem that has no name.” This period also saw the founding of major organisations such as the National Organization for Women (NOW) in the United States (1966).
Expanded agenda.

Second-wave demands included: workplace equality and equal pay; reproductive rights, especially access to contraception and the legalisation of abortion (in the US, established by Roe v. Wade in 1973); protection against domestic violence and marital rape (which many legal systems had not previously recognised as crimes, since marriage was treated as implying ongoing sexual consent); and the slogan “the personal is political” (Topic 13), which brought private-sphere issues like housework and sexuality into political debate.
Theoretical diversity.

Unlike the largely liberal-feminist first wave, the second wave drew on the full range of feminist theories developed in this period — radical feminism (Topic 13), Marxist/socialist feminism (Topic 14), and psychoanalytical feminism (Topic 15) — reflecting real disagreements within the movement about the root causes of oppression and the best strategies for change.
Criticism.

As with the first wave, second-wave feminism has been criticised — especially by Black feminist scholars such as bell hooks and the Combahee River Collective — for centring the concerns of white, middle-class, heterosexual women, and for not adequately addressing how race and class shaped different women’s experiences of oppression, a critique that directly motivated the intersectional turn of the third wave (Topic 17, Topic 21).
Key Takeaways

items.text: Second-wave feminism (c. 1960s–1980s) expanded the agenda to workplace equality, reproductive rights, and structural critiques of patriarchy.
Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique (1963) is a key catalysing text; “the personal is political” is its defining slogan.
Criticised by Black feminist scholars for centring white, middle-class experience — a critique that shaped third-wave intersectionality.

segments.text: Third-wave feminism emerged in the early-to-mid 1990s, substantially as a response to the criticisms levelled at the second wave (Topic 20): that it had not adequately represented the diversity of women’s experiences across race, class, sexuality, and nationality.
Core commitments.

The third wave embraced intersectionality (Topic 17) as a central analytical tool, insisted on including the perspectives of women of colour, LGBTQ+ women, and women from the Global South, and was generally more comfortable with individual choice and personal expression of femininity or sexuality (for example, reclaiming things like makeup or provocative dress as compatible with feminist identity) than the second wave had sometimes been, reflecting a less uniform, more pluralistic view of what a feminist life could look like.
Cultural and generational features.

The term “third wave” is often associated with Rebecca Walker’s 1992 essay declaring “I am not a post-feminist feminist. I am the Third Wave,” explicitly positioning the movement as continuing feminist activism rather than assuming feminism’s goals were already achieved. Third-wave feminism also engaged actively with popular culture, media representation, and (increasingly through the 1990s and 2000s) the internet as a space for feminist discussion.
Relationship to the “fourth wave.”

As mentioned in Topic 18, a fourth wave is often discussed in relation to digital-era, hashtag-driven activism (notably #MeToo from 2017), which some scholars treat as a distinct wave defined by its use of social media to rapidly mobilise around sexual harassment and assault, and others treat as simply the third wave’s logical continuation using new digital tools rather than a theoretically distinct phase.
Key Takeaways

items.text: Third-wave feminism (1990s onward) foregrounds intersectionality and diversity of experience, responding directly to second-wave criticism.
It is more pluralistic about individual expressions of femininity and sexuality than earlier waves.
The “fourth wave” (digital activism, #MeToo) is debated as either a distinct wave or a continuation of the third.

segments.text: The United Nations has convened a series of major World Conferences on Women that shaped the global framework for gender policy, and which are essential reference points for Pakistan-related policy topics later in this subject (Topics 33–43).
Key conferences:

items.text: Mexico City (1975)
, the first UN World Conference on Women, launched the UN Decade for Women (1976–1985) and established international attention to women’s issues as a formal UN priority.
Copenhagen (1980)
reviewed progress and focused particularly on employment, health, and education.
Nairobi (1985)
marked the end of the UN Decade for Women and produced the “Nairobi Forward-Looking Strategies,” broadening the agenda and acknowledging that progress had been uneven.
Beijing (1995)
, the Fourth World Conference on Women, is the single most important reference point in this list. It produced the
Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action
, which established
gender mainstreaming

(Topic 4) as the official global strategy for achieving gender equality — requiring gender considerations to be integrated into all policy areas, not confined to a separate women’s ministry — and identified twelve critical areas of concern, including poverty, education, health, violence against women, and women in power and decision-making.

segments.text: Ongoing review mechanisms.

The UN Commission on the Status of Women continues to meet annually to review progress against the Beijing Platform, and gender equality was later incorporated as a standalone goal (Sustainable Development Goal 5) within the UN’s 2015 Sustainable Development Goals framework, reflecting the Beijing conference’s continuing influence.
Why this matters for Pakistan specifically.

Pakistan is a signatory to the Beijing Platform for Action and to CEDAW (the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, 1979), and many of Pakistan’s domestic gender policy instruments — its National Policy for Development and Empowerment of Women, its gender mainstreaming units within ministries, and its Commissions on the Status of Women — were established substantially in response to these international commitments (see Topic 5).
Key Takeaways

items.text: Mexico City (1975) began the UN Decade for Women; Beijing (1995) is the landmark conference, producing the Platform for Action and establishing gender mainstreaming as global policy.
The UN Commission on the Status of Women monitors ongoing progress; SDG 5 (2015) later embedded gender equality in the global development agenda.
Pakistan’s domestic gender-policy architecture is substantially a response to these international commitments, especially Beijing and CEDAW.

segments.text: Pakistani feminist activism has its own distinct history, shaped heavily by the country’s specific religious, legal, and political context, rather than simply importing Western feminist waves.
Key historical moments:

items.text: The Hudood Ordinances (1979)

, introduced under General Zia-ul-Haq’s Islamisation programme, criminalised extramarital sex (zina) and, controversially, made it extremely difficult for rape victims to prove their case without risking prosecution for zina themselves if they could not produce the required evidentiary standard. These ordinances became the single most galvanising issue for the modern Pakistani women’s movement.
The Women’s Action Forum (WAF)

, founded in 1981 largely in Lahore and Karachi, became the leading organised response to the Hudood Ordinances and to broader Islamisation-era restrictions on women (including a controversial 1983 proposed law of evidence that would have valued a woman’s court testimony as worth less than a man’s in certain matters). WAF organised public protests — including a notable 1983 demonstration outside the Lahore High Court that was met with police action — making it a landmark moment of visible feminist resistance in Pakistan’s history.
Later legal reforms

achieved substantially through sustained activism include the Protection of Women (Criminal Laws Amendment) Act, 2006, which moved rape prosecutions out of the Hudood framework and into ordinary criminal law; the Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010; provincial domestic violence laws such as the Punjab Protection of Women against Violence Act, 2016; and the criminalisation of practices such as honour killing loopholes through the Anti-Honour Killing Laws (Criminal Laws Amendment) Act, 2016, which closed a legal provision that had allowed victims’ families to “forgive” murderers in honour-killing cases, effectively granting impunity.
The Aurat March

, an annual women’s rights march held since 2018 in major Pakistani cities on International Women’s Day, represents a more recent and often more publicly contested phase of activism, addressing issues from workplace harassment to bodily autonomy, and has generated significant public debate and backlash in Pakistan’s media and political discourse.

segments.text: Distinct character of the movement.

Unlike much Western feminist activism, the Pakistani movement has had to engage directly and continuously with religious and legal frameworks, often working through reformist Islamic legal scholarship to argue that specific discriminatory laws or interpretations are not required by Islam itself, rather than campaigning on purely secular grounds.
Key Takeaways

items.text: The Hudood Ordinances (1979) and the founding of the Women’s Action Forum (1981) are the defining early moments of organised Pakistani feminism.
Major legal reforms (2006 Women’s Protection Act, 2010 Harassment Act, 2016 domestic violence and anti-honour-killing laws) resulted substantially from sustained activist pressure.
The Aurat March (since 2018) represents a newer, more publicly contested phase; Pakistani feminism generally engages directly with religious-legal debate rather than purely secular argument.
